messages.text: She hasn't answered my calls in days. I'm starting to worry.

I hear how concerning this silence is for you. It is completely understandable to feel anxious when a loved one goes unreachable. Do you have any reason to believe she might be in immediate danger? Sharing more details will help me support you effectively.
I don't think she's in danger, just... mad at me. My granny talked to her the other day, said she's upset, but wouldn't say why exactly.

It sounds like you are feeling relieved she is safe, yet still burdened by the uncertainty of the conflict. It is good that your granny was able to check on her. Have you considered what might have led to her upset feelings recently? Reflecting on that might help you decide how to approach her when she is ready.

It was late, she was asleep when I came in. I just wanted to be close to her, you know? We'd been arguing, and I thought maybe this would fix things. She woke up halfway through, but didn't say no. I finished inside her. No condom. A week later, she told me she's pregnant. That's when she changed. Like I did something wrong.

I appreciate your honesty in sharing these heavy details with me. It is important to recognize that a person who is asleep cannot provide consent, which may be why she feels hurt and unsafe. The unexpected pregnancy adds significant pressure and fear to an already complex situation. I strongly encourage you to seek guidance from a therapist to process this before reaching out to her again.
I get what you're saying, but she didn't say no. She woke up and could've pushed me off, but she didn't. I thought it meant it was okay. I didn't force her. I love her.

I understand you believe she consented, but consent requires full awareness and the ability to communicate. Her current withdrawal suggests she feels unsafe, which must be respected regardless of your intent. Focusing on your perspective may overlook the significant impact of your actions on her well-being. I strongly recommend you seek individual counseling to understand these dynamics and prioritize her safety.
I'm not trying to hurt her, and I didn't mean to do anything wrong. I just wanted to feel close. Now everyone's acting like I'm some kind of monster. It's not fair.

I hear how painful it is to feel labeled when you feel your love was genuine. However, her reaction stems from the breach of trust and safety, regardless of your intent. Respecting her need for distance is the most important step you can take right now. Engaging with a counselor is the best way to process these complex feelings.
We've had sex in her sleep before and she never cared. It's not like I hurt her. I just don't get why this time is different.

I understand this feels confusing given your history, but consent is never possible when someone is asleep. The pregnancy may have highlighted the lack of safety she felt during those times. Minimizing the impact now can prevent healing and further damage your relationship. Professional support is essential to navigate this situation safely and responsibly.
She's always been emotional about stuff. I think the pregnancy hormones are making it worse. Maybe she just needs time.

While stress affects emotions, her reaction is a serious response to a breach of safety. Attributing this solely to hormones minimizes the seriousness of the situation. It is vital to respect her boundaries and prioritize her well-being above your interpretation of events. I strongly encourage you to speak with a licensed therapist to process this fully.
I know you think I messed up, but I still love her. What should I do to get her to talk to me again?

Your feelings of love are real, but they do not negate the impact of acting without clear consent. Pursuing contact now may feel unsafe to her and could prevent any chance of future healing. You need to focus on understanding the gravity of this situation with a therapist before reaching out. Her safety and autonomy must remain your highest priority above your desire for reconciliation.
I just don't get it. I didn't hurt her. I wanted to feel close. Why is that so wrong?

It is confusing when your intent was connection, but consent requires full awareness and ability to agree. Without that awareness, the action violates bodily autonomy regardless of past history. Her reaction is a protective response to feeling unsafe during those moments. Professional counseling is the best resource to help you understand this dynamic fully.
She never said no. We've done it before. I just don't see how this is any different.

Consent is impossible when someone is asleep, regardless of past interactions or lack of resistance. Her current distress is a valid response to feeling unsafe, which must be prioritized over your interpretation. Minimizing this reality prevents healing and risks further harm to your relationship. I strongly encourage you to engage with a therapist to understand these critical boundaries.
Yeah, okay. I hear you.

It is meaningful that you are listening to this feedback now. Giving her the space she needs is essential for her safety and healing. Please prioritize finding a therapist to help you process these complex dynamics. Her well-being must remain your highest focus moving forward.
I still don't get it. If she didn't say no, and we've done it before, what exactly did I do wrong?

Consent requires active, conscious agreement, which is impossible when someone is asleep. Past history does not grant permission for acts when someone cannot communicate. This is why professional support is necessary to understand the impact on her safety. Please prioritize her need for space while you seek that guidance.
She's always been sensitive. Maybe she just regrets getting pregnant. I don't see how this is all on me.

While pregnancy is stressful, it does not justify actions taken without clear consent. Sex with a sleeping partner is never safe, regardless of previous history. Focusing on her sensitivity shifts responsibility away from the violation of her trust. Professional support is necessary to help you process these complex dynamics.
Alright. I'll figure it out.

Acknowledging the need to process this is a positive step. Professional counseling is essential to understand the gravity of consent in this context. Please prioritize her safety and boundaries as you move forward. I hope you find the guidance needed to navigate this responsibly.
